To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the development of genotypic resistance against protease inhibitors in patients treated with a protease‐based triple‐drug therapy is frequent and occurs in a relevant proportion (41.4%); (2) the emergence of resistance to proteases is associated with a lower virological response to treatment; (3) the rate of development of resistance increases linearly with time; (4) the emergence of protease inhibitor resistance does not prevent a sustained increase in CD4 lymphocyte
the development of resistance to PI is associated with a worse virological response to treatment, but not to the immunological one, and it is more common in patients starting with high viral loads.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the emergence of resistance to proteases in HIV‐1 patients under triple‐drug antiretrovial therapy (HAART).
the study of the development of drug resistance in HIV‐1 infected patients under triple‐drug regimens in clinical practice, and its impact on the clinical outcome.
the development and significance of resistance of the HIV-1 virus in HIV-infected patients who are on triple-drug therapy.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the protease inhibitors have revolutionized the treatment of HIV infection, and that they have changed the natural history of the disease.

the rate of development of resistance is higher than previously reported, and that it is a major cause of treatment failure in patients adherent to therapy, but that the rate of resistance is not high enough to preclude long‐term triple drug therapy as a standard approach in the treatment of HIV‐1 infection.
the rate of resistance development is high, but the impact of resistance on the clinical course of the infection is still unclear.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
protease inhibitor resistance develops in about a third of patients treated with protease inhibitors and that it has a negative impact on virological response to treatment.

protease inhibitor resistance develops in a relevant number of patients under long-term triple-drug therapy in clinical practice, is associated with virolological treatment failure, and limits CD4 cell increase.

the rate of development of resistance in our patients was lower than that previously reported in clinical trials and was associated with a lower virological response and a limitation of the CD4 cell count increase.
The main takeaway from our work is that
protease inhibitor resistance is a major issue in clinical practice.
resistance to protease inhibitor is common, and it is not a good prognostic factor.
protease inhibitors resistance develops frequently under triple‐drug antiretrovirus therapy, and is associated with a lower treatment response.
